title: Διογένης καὶ φαλακρός
part: Diogenes and the Bald Man (Chambry 97 · Perry 248)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 97 (= Perry 248). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Διογένης ὁ κυνικὸς φιλόσοφος λοιδορούμενος ὑπό τινος φαλακροῦ εἶπεν· « Ἐγὼ μὲν οὐ λοιδορῶ· μὴ γένοιτο· ἐπαινῶ δὲ τὰς τρίχας ὅτι κρανίου κακοῦ ἀπηλλάγησαν. »
sentences.tr: Diogenēs ho kynikos philosophos loidoroumenos hypo tinos phalakrou eipen· « Egō men ou loidorō· mē genoito· epainō de tas trichas hoti kraniou kakou apēllagēsan. »
sentences.l: Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, being reviled by a certain bald man, said: « I for my part do not revile — may it not be; but I praise the hairs, because they got free of a bad skull. »
sentences.i: Diogenes the Cynic philosopher, when a bald man was abusing him, said: « I am not abusing anyone — heaven forbid; I am praising his hairs, for having got clear of a bad skull. »
sentences.n: Diogenes of Sinope, of the fourth century, is the most famous of the Cynics; the fable-book keeps a handful of these anecdotes among the animal tales. μὴ γένοιτο is an optative of wish used as a formula of horrified denial. ἀπηλλάγησαν is the aorist passive of ἀπαλλάσσω and takes a genitive of separation: the hairs escaped from the skull. Ἐγὼ μὲν οὐ λοιδορῶ is answered by ἐπαινῶ δέ — he never insults the man, only compliments the hair on deserting him, which is worse. Chambry prints no moral for this one: the piece ends at the closing quotation, and the white space below it on the page is his. Nothing has dropped out — this is a chreia, an anecdote built to land on its retort, and an epimythium would only explain the joke. Epimythia are in any case widely held to be later additions to the collections rather than part of the oldest layer, so their absence is often the older state of a piece, not a defect in it.
